title: Medical automation: Product counts overstate distinct innovation
desc: Treats successive versions cautiously and uses the inventory for device-level inquiry rather than professional-replacement claims.

kps.k: The FDA inventory documents a long regulatory history of AI-enabled medical devices, not evidence that AI replaces professionals.
kps.d: The Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Device List supplies a factual reference point: its extracts span September 1995 to March 2026 and identify devices, manufacturers, specialties and regulatory records. It presents neither competing arguments nor predictions, and supplies no measurements of clinical performance, adoption, productivity or workforce effects. Its contribution to the debate is therefore evidence of listed technologies over time, not proof of clinical autonomy or professional substitution.

kps.k: The listed applications cover varied clinical tasks and specialties rather than a single model of medical automation.
kps.d: Radiology dominates the supplied extracts, with systems for imaging, triage, segmentation, contouring and assessment. The list also includes cardiovascular, neurological, ophthalmic, pathology, surgical and other classifications. These classifications establish breadth within the inventory; they do not by themselves establish clinical indications, effectiveness or how much human oversight each device requires.

kps.k: Successive product versions make raw entry counts an unreliable proxy for distinct innovations or adoption.
kps.d: Radformation's AutoContour appears as RADAC V2 in 2022, V3 in 2023, V4 in 2024 and V5 in 2026. Analysts must distinguish regulatory records, product versions and product families before counting distinct technologies. Recurrent listings do not independently demonstrate wider deployment or faster market growth.

kps.k: The inventory supports device-level regulatory investigation, but further evidence must establish clinical and operational implications.
kps.d: Links distinguish K-numbered premarket notification records, DEN-numbered De Novo records and P-numbered premarket approval records, including supplements. The practical use is to trace a particular device and its regulatory pathway rather than treat every listing as an equivalent approval or performance finding. Claims about comparative effectiveness, autonomous use or changes in professional work require evidence beyond these entries.

vlens.an: The selected regulatory source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by functioning as a device-level inventory rather than evidence of clinical autonomy, adoption, performance or professional replacement. Most directly, its separate entries for successive AutoContour versions show that raw listing totals can count iterations within one product family and therefore overstate distinct innovation. The inventory’s breadth across specialties and regulatory record types also reinforces the need for product-specific investigation rather than aggregate workforce conclusions. There is little internal variation in viewpoint because the source does not advance an argumentative position: variation lies instead in devices, versions, specialties and pathways. Nothing in the supplied material challenges the cluster’s cautious interpretation, but this conclusion concerns this curated source alone and should not be generalized to all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

elens.an: The 2026-period evidence supports the proposition’s cautious treatment of FDA inventory counts. The inventory records device entries and regulatory links, but does not supply clinical-performance, adoption, productivity or workforce evidence; it therefore supports device-level investigation rather than claims that AI is replacing medical professionals. Most directly, the recurring AutoContour family—from RADAC V2 in 2022 to RADAC V5 in 2026—shows that separate entries can represent successive versions of the same product family, so raw listing totals are not reliable measures of distinct innovation or market growth. There is no substantive internal disagreement in the supplied evidence: the only source is an administrative inventory rather than an argumentative source. Its material variation lies in the breadth of specialties, tasks and regulatory record types represented, none of which resolves effectiveness, autonomy or professional-substitution questions. Because this is one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of regulators or medical-device stakeholders generally.

parents.t: Medical AI device inventories: regulatory breadth does not establish innovation or impact
